events.text: Ding! Remnant detected. After a war of the pantheons a fallen god drifts at the edge of your domain like ash over a cold hearth: Ashen Ilgwang, a sun that burned out. "Edible," says the System. A god in grey sets down an abacus of black stones beside it. {npc}, of the Silent Hall. "Everything eaten in heaven is counted," {he} says. "And every meal, your own domain withers a little."

effects.log: {npc} moves one black stone. "Honest," {he} says, which in the Silent Hall is nearly a compliment.

choices.text: Ask what the withering looks like

effects.log: "Incense that burns short. Shrines that go a little cold," says {npc}. "Tend them after a meal and it eases." You remember that.
{npc} turns it back up without a word and moves a stone anyway. The Silent Hall does not need your leave to count.

events.text: {npc} of the Silent Hall stops you on the steps of heaven, the abacus of black stones under one arm. One stone is already moved. "It is yours," {he} says, "from another life. A god who gave the hunger its own throne. The Domain Maw." {He} frowns at it. "The Hall never forgets a meal. I find I never forgot you."

choices.text: Say the throne was yours to give

effects.log: "Then give it again, and better," says {npc}, and for once the Silent Hall smiles.
The System says, very low: "I remember the throne." It sounds less hungry for saying it.

events.text: The System makes an offer. "Eat faster. Your domain grows back." {npc} has an older rule, written on the Silent Hall's door: one meal, then one year of tending what the meal withered. Below, your shrines are already a shade colder. A priestess, Ma Ok-hui, has started lighting two sticks of incense where one used to do.

effects.log: One meal, one year of tending. The System sulks. {npc} moves a white stone, the first you have seen.
You eat as fast as the hunger likes. Your strength grows; Ma Ok-hui lights three sticks now, then four.

choices.text: Argue the Hall into a softer rule

ok.log: {npc} hears you out and changes one word on the door: tending, not penance. The rule is the same and lighter.

fail.log: {npc} hears you out and changes nothing. You keep the rule anyway, a little sour.

events.text: Sorrowless Hae, a goddess whose sea dried up, is falling. The goddess's priests below still pray to a sea that is not there. "If you eat Hae," says {npc}, "those prayers have nowhere left to go." Across the cloud a god of the Throne of Storms is already reaching for Hae. The System is reaching faster.

choices.text: Gather Hae's prayers first, then eat

effects.log: You catch the prayers like rain in cupped hands and take them into your own shrines. Then you eat, gently. {npc} counts both.

choices.text: Eat Hae before the storm god can

effects.log: The sea's whole memory pours into you, salt and bright. Hae's prayers scatter. The storm god looks at you the way {npc} does.

events.text: The faithful road is slow and cold. Each meal costs your domain a year of tending, and the shrines of {b10_pantheon} gossip that you have gone thin. Ma Ok-hui writes up on the smoke: is the god still there? {npc} comes by with the abacus and does not move a stone. "You are paying," {he} says. "The Hall notices who pays."

effects.log: You warm Ma Ok-hui's shrine with your own hands for a season. The incense burns tall again, and the withering eases.

choices.text: Send Ma Ok-hui a sign, at a price

effects.log: A single warm wind through the shrine door. It costs faith you can barely spare. Ma Ok-hui weeps, and tells the town.
You let it ache. The hunger learns that it can be told no.

events.text: The hungry road has a bill. Your domain greys at the edges; Ma Ok-hui's shrine goes dark for a whole winter. And the Silent Hall closes its door to you: {npc} reads the verdict aloud on the steps. "Every god in {b10_pantheon} will hide their dead from you now. I counted. It was a great deal."

ok.log: {npc} looks away first. The door stays shut, but nobody in the Hall laughs at you again.

fail.log: The Hall's silence is heavier than you are. You leave the steps with your domain aching.

effects.log: You pour faith into the grey edges until they green. {npc} moves a white stone, reluctantly.
"Count with me for a year," {he} says. You do. It is very boring. The door opens a crack.

events.text: Ding! Three remnants devoured. A sun, a sea, a drum: they sit inside you and do not quarrel. "I do not want to be a mouth on your throne any more," says the System. "I want a throne of my own." {npc} sets the abacus down and, for the first time, does not count. "Give it one," {he} says, "and it will stop eating your domain to feed itself."

choices.text: Give the hunger its own seat

effects.log: You build it a throne out of everything it ate, and it climbs up, and it is quiet.
{npc} stands beside the new throne with the abacus shut. "Witnessed," {he} says. "The Hall will write it."

choices.text: Seat it, but keep it on a chain

effects.log: You give it a throne with a short chain. It grumbles and accepts. Some hungers like a fence.

events.text: The hunger rises in you like a tide with no moon to pull it back. The remnants inside you, the sun, the sea, the drum, are arguing. {npc} has come, against the Hall's verdict, and stands just out of reach. "It wants a throne," {he} says. "Give it one, or it will make one of you."

effects.log: You build the hunger its seat out of the three remnants before it can build one out of you. It sits, and the tide goes out.

ok.log: "A throne," it agrees, "and I will eat less of yours." It keeps the bargain, mostly.

fail.log: It does not bargain. It just climbs onto the throne you hurry to build, still chewing.

events.text: {npc} comes once more, the abacus wrapped in grey cloth. "There is one meal left that the hunger could eat," {he} says. "The god who carries it. If you let it, you would become a domain of hunger itself. Every god after you would feed you a little, and you would never take again." {He} unwraps the abacus. "I would count that one. Gladly."

choices.text: Say you will think on it

effects.log: "Think a century," says {npc}. "The Hall can wait."
{npc} bows. It is a very small bow, and the Silent Hall talks about it for years.

events.text: {npc} sits on the Silent Hall's shut door and talks to you through the crack. "If the hunger ate the last god it can reach, itself, and you with it," {he} says, "I would write one word after your name. Sated." A stone clicks. "It is not the worst word. The ledger asks first. It always asks first."

effects.log: {npc} opens it a hand's width. It is more than the Hall has opened for anyone in an age.

choices.text: Say the word sounds like rest

effects.log: "It does," says {npc}. "That is why I count so carefully."

events.text: Ding! Sign-in place found: a shrine with your name on it. In the Register of heaven every shrine raised to a god is a line, and {npc} keeps the lesser lines, the hillside altars and the roadside stones. {He} wipes ink off {his} fingers. "Sign in at a shrine and it pays," {he} says. "Tend it and it pays more. Forget it and it stops. Most gods forget."

choices.text: Ask {him} to show you the forgotten ones

effects.log: {npc} turns the Register to the back pages. Hundreds of little shrines, their ink gone pale. One is yours.
"The grand ones, at first," says {npc}. "The small ones, in the end." {He} does not explain.
You sign. A bell rings somewhere far below, and a little faith climbs up the smoke.

events.text: {npc} opens the Register and stops. A line in old ink, in a hand {he} knows is {his} own: a god who once signed in at every shrine raised to them and kept a calendar of altars. "The Shrine Calendar," {he} reads. "That was you, in a life before. I kept your ink." {He} looks up. "I am glad you came back to sign."

effects.log: Your new ink sits next to the old. The Register warms like a hand. {npc} smiles.

choices.text: Ask what you did wrong last time

effects.log: "Nothing," says {npc}. "You were only late once. Do not be late."

events.text: Two shrines want you this year. On a cloud ford, a great new shrine of {b10_pantheon}, with bells and a hundred priests. On a hill below, the old stone of Gu Bok-nam, a shrine-sweeper who has swept it for fifty years and never once seen a sign. {npc} says nothing. {He} only holds the brush out to you.

choices.text: Sign in at the old stone

effects.log: You sign at Gu Bok-nam's stone. Gu Bok-nam feels it in the broom and sits down on the step and laughs.

choices.text: Sign in at the great shrine

effects.log: A hundred bells ring for you. The faith is loud and quick. Gu Bok-nam sweeps on.

events.text: The Register is full, {npc} tells you: a god may keep only so many lines. To raise new shrines you would have to strike out the old. Dal-i, a child below, rings the bell of one of your oldest altars every morning and has never missed. "The child's line is small," says {npc}. "It is also the only one that never stops."

choices.text: Keep the small lines, raise none

effects.log: You keep every old line. {npc} writes a note in the margin: kept. Dal-i rings the bell.

choices.text: Strike the small ones for grander shrines

effects.log: You strike out three faint lines. New shrines rise, rich and loud. {npc} blots the ink very carefully.

events.text: Small shrines are slow. Each pays a little and wants a lot of tending: a roof re-thatched by a wind you send, a spring kept flowing. The grand gods of {b10_pantheon} laugh at the size of your Register. {npc} climbs the hill with you to Gu Bok-nam's stone and helps you sweep, which a keeper of the Register is not supposed to do.

choices.text: Mend the roof with a wind

effects.log: A warm wind, a straight roof. The stone pays a little more each year it is tended.
You say it together, badly. Gu Bok-nam corrects you both.
They laugh. The small shrines go on paying. You learn which sound lasts longer.

events.text: The grand shrines pay loud and fade fast: their priests want miracles, and the lines you struck out cannot be written back. Dal-i's bell has stopped; the child rings it at another god's altar now. {npc} brings you the Register open at the blot. "Abandoned shrines stop paying," {he} says. "So do abandoned keepers."

choices.text: Write the old line back, at a cost

effects.log: It takes a great deal of faith to make old ink take again. It takes. {npc} breathes out.

ok.log: You send the child a dream of the old altar. Next morning the bell rings for you again.

fail.log: The child sleeps through the dream. The bell rings for someone else.

choices.text: Say grand shrines are worth it

effects.log: "They are worth a great deal," says {npc}. "For a while."

events.text: Ding! Four shrines signed. The Register turns its own pages for you: each shrine has become a date, and the dates make a year. "A calendar," breathes {npc}. "Of altars. Every day of heaven, somewhere, a shrine that is yours." Far below, Gu Bok-nam and Dal-i hear their bells ring on the same morning.

choices.text: Give the first date to the old stone

effects.log: The calendar opens on Gu Bok-nam's stone. {npc} writes it in with {his} best brush.

choices.text: Sign in at all four at once

effects.log: You sign four times in one breath. The calendar holds. It pays half again from now on.
You read every date. Each one is a person sweeping, ringing, waiting.

events.text: The grand shrines and the few small ones left all ring at once, and the Register rearranges itself into a calendar of altars. {npc} reads it with {his} lips tight. "It is a fine calendar," {he} says. "It has gaps where the struck lines were. Heaven will see them."

choices.text: Fill a gap with a new small shrine

effects.log: You raise a stone on a hill nobody prays on, and sign in. One gap closes.
The calendar keeps its gaps. Every year, on those days, you feel a little cold.

events.text: {npc} closes the Register gently. "Every shrine raised to you has signed you in," {he} says. "You could sign one last time and stay. Be the altar the next gods sign in at. Something would always sign them back." {He} smiles. "I would keep that line myself, at the front of the book."

choices.text: Say you are not ready to be an altar

effects.log: "Nobody is," says {npc}. "That is why it asks."

choices.text: Ask who would keep Gu Bok-nam's stone

effects.log: "I would," says {npc}. "I have been practising the sweeping."

events.text: {npc} finds you counting the grand shrines. "You could sign in at the last of them," {he} says, "and close the Register behind you. The shrines would still be tended. Nobody would sign." {He} touches the blot on the old page. "I would rather you did not. But the ledger asks first, not me."

choices.text: Promise to sign the small ones too

effects.log: You promise. {npc} writes the promise in the margin, which is the same as a vow.

choices.text: Say a closed book is restful

effects.log: "For the book," says {npc}.

events.text: Ding! The System re-binds. The sect was handed on long ago, at the second gate; now it reads a temple order. Its first window opens over a young priest sweeping your hall: [Appraisal: {npc}. Hidden gift: Lamp-Heart.] {He} looks up, sees nothing, and keeps sweeping. "Somebody," {he} says to the empty hall, "is going to need a temple order."
events.arc: The Temple Order of a Domain

effects.log: A small light settles on {npc}'s shoulder. {He} stops sweeping and bows to the air. Your first priest.

choices.text: Read the rest of the window

effects.log: [Goals: found the order, ordain three, raise a hall, work three miracles.] It is a very long window.
{npc} sweeps the whole hall and then the steps. Lamp-Heart, the System says. You believe it.

events.text: {npc}, a young priest in your hall, lights the first lamp of the morning and freezes. "I dreamt of you," {he} says to the air. "Another life. A High Temple, and a god who became the lamp on its altar." {He} laughs at the dream. "I am too young to dream old things." The System appraises {him} and says: (Lamp-Heart. Again.)
events.arc: The Temple Order of a Domain

effects.log: The light finds {npc} as if it had only gone out for a moment.
{npc} writes it down on the back of a prayer slip and keeps it in {his} sleeve.

events.text: The order grows, and the System appraises every new priest. One window is red: [Choi Han-gyeol. Hidden gift: Light Fingers. Steals from offerings.] Han-gyeol is the best singer in the hall. {npc} has seen the window too, somehow, and comes to you. "I can mend Han-gyeol," {he} says. "Or you can cast Han-gyeol out, and the order will be faster."
events.arc: The Temple Order of a Domain

choices.text: Keep Han-gyeol, let {npc} mend the habit

effects.log: Han-gyeol is given the offering bowls to guard. Han-gyeol blushes for a year and steals nothing. {npc} is very proud.

choices.text: Cast Han-gyeol out and drive the order on

effects.log: Han-gyeol goes down the mountain with their songs. The order is cleaner, and quieter. {npc} says nothing at all.

events.text: [Goal: work three miracles.] A town below, Seoha, has a well gone dry. The order could pray a miracle slowly, with every priest, and keep the town's faith for a generation. Or you could work it at once, a god's hand on a dry stone, and move on to the next goal. {npc} has already started rolling up {his} sleeves.
events.arc: The Temple Order of a Domain

choices.text: Let the order pray it slowly

effects.log: Nine days of prayer, and the well fills on the tenth. Seoha raises a hall to the order.
The well fills in a breath. Seoha cheers and forgets the priests. The goal ticks.

events.text: A gentle order is a slow one. Han-gyeol's songs fill the hall, but the goals tick like a water clock. Gods of {b10_pantheon} with bigger orders smile at yours. {npc} sits up nights with the ledgers, appraising priests by lamplight, and falls asleep on a prayer slip.
events.arc: The Temple Order of a Domain

effects.log: It is a small miracle, and nobody counts it. {npc} wakes warm and works twice as hard.
You read three windows. One hides Healer's Hands. The order is richer by a gift.

choices.text: Let the goals take their time

effects.log: They take it. Each one, when it comes, is solid.

events.text: A hard order is a fast one. The goals tick: halls, priests, miracles. But {npc} has stopped lighting the first lamp with a song. Down the mountain, Han-gyeol sings in another god's temple, and the faithful there are many. "Do you still trust me?" {npc} asks you one morning. It is the first time {he} has doubted.
events.arc: The Temple Order of a Domain

effects.log: {npc} lights the lamp with a song again. It is a little shaky.

ok.log: Han-gyeol comes up the mountain with their songs and a promise to keep their fingers still.

fail.log: Han-gyeol stays where they are. They send one song up, which is something.

choices.text: Say trust is not a goal

effects.log: {npc} looks at the System's window for a long moment. "No," {he} says. "It is not."

events.text: Ding! Temple Order goal: the fifth. The halls ring at once; every lamp in the order lights itself. Out of the light a High Temple stands on the summit of your domain, as if it had always been there. {npc} drops the broom. "We built that?" {he} asks. "We built that," says the System, which is not like it.
events.arc: The Temple Order of a Domain

effects.log: {npc} holds the High Temple's key in both hands and cannot speak.
You name every hidden gift in the order. Each priest glows as you do. Their gifts pay twice from now on.
You stand on the top step of the High Temple and look down at what a temple order is.

events.text: The fifth goal arrives in a hard year, and the High Temple rises over a quieter order. {npc} carries the lamp up the new steps alone. At the top {he} stops. "It is beautiful," {he} says. "I wish the hall had sung for it."
events.arc: The Temple Order of a Domain

effects.log: A god singing, off-key, at the top of {his} own temple. {npc} laughs, and joins in.
"It is a great deal," says {npc}. {He} lights the lamp.

events.text: {npc} lights the High Temple's lamp and sits beside it. "The order could keep your domain without you now," {he} says. "You could become this lamp. The light every priest lights first." {He} cups {his} hands around the flame. "I would light you every dawn. I would never forget a single one."
events.arc: The Temple Order of a Domain

effects.log: {npc} nods. The flame stands very straight.
"Then I will light it for you anyway," says {npc}.

events.text: {npc}, who once asked if you still trusted {him}, holds the High Temple's lamp. "If you gave the domain to me," {he} says slowly, "a priest who doubted you, and became the lamp, I would not let it go out. Not once. That is what doubting teaches." {He} looks at the flame. "The ledger will ask you. Not me."
events.arc: The Temple Order of a Domain

effects.log: {npc} laughs, surprised, and the doubt goes out of {his} face.

choices.text: Say the lamp is safe with {him}

effects.log: "It is," says {npc}. "So are you."

events.text: Ding! The Mirror opens at a gathering of the heavens. On the cloud stage a young god, {npc}, works {his} one miracle: a bell rung once that rings twice, the second time in every heart that heard the first. The Mirror ripples. [Copied, partly.] {npc} turns, and looks straight at you through a thousand gods.
events.arc: The Mirror Sees a Domain's Miracle

effects.log: {npc} bows back, stiffly. "You saw it," {he} says. "Everybody saw it. Not everybody kept it."
You watch the bell again in memory, and the Mirror fills in what it missed. {npc}'s eyes narrow.
You go before {he} can reach you. The Mirror hums all the way home.

events.text: {npc}, a young god who rings a bell that rings twice, finds you before the gathering begins. "I dreamt a god with a mirror copied every miracle of the pantheons once," {he} says, "and borrowed them so well nobody minded. You have that god's face." {He} folds {his} arms. "Do not copy mine. Or ask first."
events.arc: The Mirror Sees a Domain's Miracle

effects.log: "Ask what?" says {npc}, and then, after a long time: "Yes." The Mirror ripples, politely.
{npc} nods as if {he} expected it. "Then I will watch you watching."

events.text: At the Gathering of the Spring Equinox, Saengmo, Mother of Seeds, wakes a field of seeds with one breath. The Mirror drinks it. {npc}, beside you, says quietly: "Gods remember who copies them. Tell Saengmo, and Saengmo may teach you. Hide it, and Saengmo may never know. Or Saengmo may, and then heaven is a small place."
events.arc: The Mirror Sees a Domain's Miracle

effects.log: Saengmo laughs, and shows you the breath properly. "Seeds like to be woken twice," Saengmo says.
You say nothing. The Mirror holds the miracle like a stolen coin, warm and quiet.

events.text: {npc} catches you in the Mirror's light, the bell miracle half-copied in it. "Give it back," {he} says. "Or work it and tell everyone whose it is. Or work it and do not. I am only one god. I am the one you copied first."
events.arc: The Mirror Sees a Domain's Miracle

effects.log: You ring the bell twice before {b10_pantheon} and say {npc}'s name. {His} faithful double that year.
The bell rings twice for you. {npc} hears it from across heaven and does not forgive it.

ok.log: The Mirror takes the rest of it in one look. {npc} goes pale. "Well," {he} says. "Name me, at least."

fail.log: The Mirror fogs. {npc} walks away before it clears, and tells nobody, which is worse.

events.text: Copying with credit is slow. Each owner wants to be asked, then thanked, then asked again. Haeryong, Keeper of Tides, keeps you a month on a beach before the Mirror is allowed to look. {npc} comes to watch you wait, and sits on the sand beside you without a word, which is a kind of word.
events.arc: The Mirror Sees a Domain's Miracle

effects.log: You wait together. Haeryong lets the Mirror look twice, out of boredom.

choices.text: Work Saengmo's seeds for a dry town

effects.log: The seeds wake, and the town thanks Saengmo and you both. It costs faith.
You learn nothing the Mirror can copy, and something it cannot.

events.text: A secret copy has a shadow. Saengmo's priests notice a dry town woke too fast. The Mirror's copies cost less every time you work them, and the owners feel each one, like a sleeve tugged in a crowd. {npc} has told nobody. {He} only sits at every gathering in the front row, looking at you.
events.arc: The Mirror Sees a Domain's Miracle

ok.log: {npc} looks away first. But {he} is back at the next one.

fail.log: You look away first. Half the gathering sees.

choices.text: Send {him} a gift of the copy

effects.log: You send {npc} a bell that rings twice, made by your own hand. {He} keeps it, and keeps watching.
The seeds wake. Somewhere Saengmo frowns at nothing.

events.text: Ding! Two miracles copied. The Mirror goes still, then soft at the edges, like water under a veil. [The Borrowed Miracle.] "It has learned to borrow," says {npc}, who has come without being asked, "instead of take. Its copies will cost you half. The owners will feel them half as often." {He} sounds as if {he} cannot decide how to feel.
events.arc: The Mirror Sees a Domain's Miracle

effects.log: {npc} looks into the softened Mirror and sees {his} own bell there, with {his} name written under it.
Seeds wake to a bell that rings twice. Heaven has not seen the like.
The Mirror ripples, embarrassed.

events.text: The Mirror veils itself, and {npc} comes up out of the gathering's front row at last. "Half as often," {he} says. "That is what the window says. The owners will feel your copies half as often." {He} holds up the bell. "I will still feel mine."
events.arc: The Mirror Sees a Domain's Miracle

effects.log: You name {npc} as the owner, aloud, at last. The Mirror writes it under the bell.
"It is," says {npc}. "I am the one paying it."

events.text: {npc} rings {his} bell once on the edge of heaven, and it rings twice. "Your Mirror could copy one last thing," {he} says. "You. And give you back to every god at once. Each pantheon would work one small miracle it could not remember learning." {He} smiles. "I think mine would be you, ringing twice."
events.arc: The Mirror Sees a Domain's Miracle

effects.log: Two bells, four rings. It is not a miracle. It is a nice afternoon.

choices.text: Say you would rather be remembered

effects.log: "You will be," says {npc}. "By the owners. We always remember."

events.text: {npc} stands at the Mirror with {his} arms folded. "If you stepped in," {he} says, "with every borrowed miracle, and gave them back one by one to their owners, the last thing it showed would be empty." {He} touches the glass. "Mine first, please. The ledger asks you before it lets you. That much is fair."
events.arc: The Mirror Sees a Domain's Miracle

effects.log: {npc} lets out a breath. "Then I can stop watching," {he} says, and almost does.
"Empty is empty," says {npc}.

events.text: Ding! [DIVINE EXPERIENCE ENABLED.] A worshipper below, the ferrywoman Song Ae-ri, pulls a drowning child out of a river in your name. [+150 EXP.] A god in a wrinkled robe drops into the seat beside your throne. {npc}. "First patch?" {he} asks. "I cleared this game once. Kept the save. Experience comes from what they do down there. Level thirty, you get a class."

effects.log: {npc} grins. "Do not grind. Watch. The good deeds come if you deserve them." {He} is mostly right.
Song Ae-ri's ferry never leaks again. Song Ae-ri ferries for free on festival days. (+150 EXP.)
It is very long. You decide not to look at it again for a while.

events.text: {npc}, a god who cleared the game once and kept the save, leans on your throne. "Funny," {he} says. "In my save file there is a god with your face who applied the last patch. The game of heaven ran without a Player after that. Fairer." {He} taps the blue window. "New game plus, then?"

effects.log: "Good," says {npc}. "You keep your settings." Experience flows a little faster.

choices.text: Ask how the old save ended

effects.log: "With a friend at your side," says {npc}, "or alone. I forget which. I always forget which."

events.text: The bar fills slowly. Worshippers' deeds feed it: a kindness here, a harvest there. {npc} shows you the other way: send your worshippers on quests. Wars, pilgrimages, a dragon nobody asked to fight. "Quick experience," {he} says. "I did that, my first run. I would not do it again. But it is your save."

effects.log: You let the deeds come as they come. The bar fills slowly, like a well.
Pilgrimages, wars, a dragon. The bar leaps. Some of the worshippers come home.

events.text: Song Ae-ri the ferrywoman is old now, and asks you in prayer for one more year on the river. The System tells you: [Granting this: 0 EXP. Sending the grandson to the war: +600 EXP.] {npc} reads the window over your shoulder and goes very quiet.

effects.log: One more year on the river. Song Ae-ri ferries everyone across for free. [0 EXP.] {npc} pats your throne.

choices.text: Send the grandson to the war

effects.log: The grandson goes, and comes home older. [+600 EXP.] Song Ae-ri does not pray to you again.

events.text: The slow road is slow. Gods who grind are level forty; you are twenty-something. {npc} plays a long game of go with you on the throne steps and loses on purpose. "Players who rush," {he} says, "clear the game and then do not know what to do with the save." Below, Song Ae-ri teaches the grandson to steer.

effects.log: The grandson steers straight. [+150 EXP.] Song Ae-ri thanks you out loud on the water.
"Kept it," {he} says. "Visit it, sometimes. It is quiet in there."

choices.text: Lose a game of go back

effects.log: You lose on purpose too. It becomes a habit.

events.text: The fast road leaves marks. Your temples are full of pilgrims with sore feet and veterans with long silences. [Level up!] [Level up!] The windows come so fast you stop reading them. {npc} stops visiting. When you find {him}, {he} is sitting in the ruins of {his} own old save, looking at something you cannot see.

effects.log: You sit in the ruins with {npc} and say nothing. {He} leans on your shoulder after a while.

choices.text: Bring the veterans home in a dream

ok.log: They dream of their own doors, and wake lighter. The dream does not count as a deed.

fail.log: The dream is only half yours. They wake confused.

effects.log: [Level up!] It is very quiet on your throne.

events.text: Ding! [LEVEL 30.] Five blue windows open around your throne like doors: Warden, Harvester, Muse, Judge, Herald. {npc} whistles. "A divine class," {he} says. "Choose well. You choose once, and the game remembers." Below, an old ferrywoman looks up at the sky and does not know why.

effects.log: "Muse," says {npc}. "I wanted something to do after the end." You think about it for a long time.

choices.text: Look at each window in turn

effects.log: Warden for the hurt, Harvester for faith, Muse for the mind, Judge for justice, Herald for fame. You will pick in the ledger.
When you open them the windows are still there, patient.

events.text: The level-thirty chime rings across heaven, and some of the gods who grinded with you clap. The five class windows open: Warden, Harvester, Muse, Judge, Herald. {npc} is not there. A note on the throne, in {his} handwriting: (GG. Choose a kind one.)

effects.log: You find {npc} in the ruins of the old save and bring {him} back to watch you choose.
You fold it into your sleeve. You will read it again before you choose.

events.text: One more window floats over your throne, very small, after the class: [THE LAST PATCH: APPLY?] {npc} looks at it and smiles. "After that the game of heaven runs without a Player," {he} says. "A little fairer. I never applied mine. I wanted to see what you would do."

choices.text: Say you will apply it someday

effects.log: "Someday is a good day," says {npc}. "I will be there."
It closes. It does not go away.

events.text: [THE LAST PATCH: APPLY?] {npc} reads it over your shoulder, back from the ruins. "If you apply it," {he} says, "apply it with somebody beside you. The last window says thank you for playing. It is nicer to hear with a friend." {He} sits down. "The ledger will ask. Take your time."

effects.log: "I kept the save," says {npc}. "I can keep a seat."
{npc} laughs. "Not yet. Not yet."

events.text: Ding! [You are a star now.] For once you are on the other side of the sky. Below, a mortal child of no account looks up and meets your light. [Host found: {npc}.] {He} is eleven, sells rice cakes in the market of Hwado, and talks to stars when nobody is listening. "Are you the one who answers?" {he} asks.

effects.log: A star twinkles twice. {npc} drops a rice cake and laughs out loud. Your host.
Valour, Mercy, Cunning, Devotion, Wonder, Ruin: the stars choose what pleases them. You will choose in the ledger.
{npc} sells the last cake to a beggar for nothing. You find that you liked that.

events.text: {npc}, a rice-cake seller in the market of Hwado, looks up at your light and frowns. "My grandmother told me of a tenth star," {he} says, "the one that answers. My grandmother said it went up from heaven a long time ago and stayed." {He} squints. "You shine like that one."

effects.log: {npc} gasps, then nods as if {he} expected it. "My grandmother said you would."
{npc} tells you {his} whole day. It is a very good day.

events.text: Other stars sponsor their hosts loudly: coins of light for every brave deed, a sulk for every timid one. {npc} is not brave. {He} is kind, and slow, and spends {his} wages on {his} neighbour's medicine. "The other stars say I am boring," {he} tells you. "Am I boring?"

effects.log: You give your taste to Mercy. {npc} glows. It is not brave. It is enough.

choices.text: Say be braver, and you will shine

effects.log: You give your taste to Valour. {npc} swallows, and goes to stand up to the market bully. {He} wins, barely.

events.text: A flood comes to Hwado. {npc} could carry {his} neighbours' children to the hill, one by one, slow and safe. Or {he} could climb the levee and hold the sluice gate shut, which is a deed a star would pay for twice and might cost {him} a broken arm. {He} looks up at you before {he} decides.

choices.text: Shine on the road to the hill

effects.log: {npc} carries nine children up the hill. Nobody sings about it. Everyone remembers.
{npc} holds the gate all night. The town is saved; {his} arm is not. A star pays twice.

events.text: A gentle host makes a quiet star. The other stars of {b10_pantheon} laugh at the small deeds you like: a medicine bought, a cake given away. They burn bright on their heroes' wars. {npc}, grown now, runs the rice-cake stall and keeps a lamp in the window for you. "I hope I am not dull," {he} says.

effects.log: {npc} laughs. The stall does well that year, which is luck you did not quite give.
{He} mends the beggar's roof. You like it. (The host pleases you.)
They laugh. You shine on the stall.

events.text: A brave host makes a bright star, and a tired host. {npc} has fought three bullies, a fire and a river this year. The arm aches in the rain. "I do it because you like it," {he} says to the sky one night. "Do you like it?"

effects.log: {npc} rests. It is the first quiet season {he} has had. {He} sleeps well.

choices.text: Heal the arm through the clouds

ok.log: The ache goes out of it one morning. {npc} looks up and says thank you.

fail.log: The light does not reach. {npc} binds the arm alone and goes on.

choices.text: Say yes, and send {him} out again

effects.log: {He} goes. {He} pleases you. (The host pleases you.)

events.text: Ding! [Your host has pleased you eight times.] Something turns in you that is not a star's light. You are not only watching now: you are answering. [Your Own Star.] Below, {npc} looks up from the rice-cake stall and sees a light that has a face, almost.

effects.log: {npc} sees it. {He} does not tell anyone. {He} puts an extra cake on the windowsill.

choices.text: Shine on all of Hwado at once

effects.log: Everybody in the market looks up on the same night. It is a good year.

choices.text: Stay a star and keep watching

effects.log: You watch. It is what stars are for, and you are good at it.

events.text: The eighth deed is the levee again, in a worse flood. {npc} holds the gate one last time, then comes down and sits in the mud and looks up at you. "That is eight," {he} says. "I counted." Something in your light turns into a face.

choices.text: Come down as far as you can

effects.log: You come down as low as a star can, and {npc} feels warm in the mud.
"Good," says {npc}, and lies back in the mud and laughs.

events.text: {npc}, older now, keeps the lamp in the stall window lit. "Grandmother said the tenth star went up for good," {he} says to the sky, "and answers mortals at night. You could be that one." {He} smiles. "I would talk to you every night. You would get very tired of my days."

effects.log: {npc} laughs and tells you about the day. It is a very good day.

choices.text: Say you are not ready to go up for good

effects.log: "Stars are never ready," says {npc}. "They just shine."

events.text: {npc} sits on the levee where {he} held the gate eight times. "If you went up as the tenth star," {he} says, "I think I would go up too, one day. Beside you. Two lights not far apart." {He} rubs the arm that aches in the rain. "The sky asks first. So do I."

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. "Then I will try not to be in a hurry."
"I know," says {npc}. "That is why I would."

events.text: Ding! The notebook opens. In a god's hand it lists the year ahead: a gathering of the heavens, a war of the pantheons, a blight on your domain. Heed a tip and pay in faith; ignore it and the domain pays instead. A herald in white snatches at the page. {npc}, keeper of the Heavenly Calendar. "Nobody reads heaven ahead," {he} says. "That is my work."

effects.log: {npc} reads it, goes pale, and reads it again. "Some of this is wrong," {he} says. "Some is not."
{npc} pulls {his} hand back and bows, very coldly. "The Calendar remembers," {he} says.
[A blight on your domain, next spring.] You read it until it means something.

events.text: {npc}, keeper of the Heavenly Calendar, holds up a page with a blank day in it. "Every year," {he} says, "heaven skips one day. My predecessor said a god once wrote themself on the last page of a notebook and tore it out." {He} looks at your notebook. "I think I have found the rest of it."

effects.log: {npc} reads the first page and laughs once. "It is kind," {he} says. "The first tip is kind."
"I keep it blank," says {npc}. "It seemed polite."

events.text: [A war of the pantheons: the Throne of Storms marches on the Green Assembly at the next equinox.] If it is true, the Calendar must be told; {npc} must ring the herald's bell. If you keep it, your pantheon could be ready and the others not. {npc} has not seen this page. {He} is waiting on the steps below.

effects.log: {npc} reads it, rings the bell, and heaven is warned. "You could have kept that," {he} says, puzzled.
You tell only your own pantheon. When the war comes, they are ready and the others are not.

events.text: The notebook is wrong sometimes. [A gathering of the heavens, the ninth month.] The Calendar says the eleventh. You can sense, faintly, whether a tip is true, if you sit with it. {npc} wants to know which of you is right. "If your book beats my Calendar," {he} says stiffly, "I want to hear it from you, not from heaven."

choices.text: Sit with the tip, and tell {him}

effects.log: You sit until you feel it: the book is right. You tell {npc} first. {He} moves the date.
The gathering comes in the ninth month. {npc} arrives late, red-faced, and does not look at you.

events.text: Sharing tips costs you the edge. Every warning you hand {npc} goes to every pantheon. Your own gods grumble that you read heaven ahead for strangers. But {npc} has started leaving the Calendar on your step each morning, open at the next week, so you can check the book against it.

effects.log: You sit with the tip and feel it. It is false. {npc} crosses it out with {his} own brush.
You pay faith to strengthen your domain's fields. The blight comes, and finds them ready.
They grumble. Nobody in heaven was surprised by the war.

events.text: A secret guide has a shadow. Your pantheon wins a war it saw coming, and the others whisper. The Calendar's dates keep being wrong where your book is right, and heaven laughs at {npc}. {He} comes to you at last, the Calendar under {his} arm. "You are making a fool of me," {he} says. "Is it worth it?"

ok.log: {npc} walks away. The next tip you keep is true, and your pantheon is grateful.

fail.log: {npc} does not walk away. {He} waits until you look down.

effects.log: {npc} takes it with both hands and says nothing for a long time.
"By ear," says {npc}, surprised. "Mostly by ear."

events.text: Ding! Three tips heeded, three come true. The notebook shakes in your hands, and every page rewrites itself in a steadier hand. [The Calendar Rewritten.] From now on every tip is true. {npc} comes up the steps with the Calendar and opens it beside the book. For the first time the two agree on every day.

effects.log: {npc} copies the first month into the Calendar with {his} best brush, and signs it with both your names.
You read the year ahead of heaven. It is mostly quiet. You are glad.

choices.text: Close the book for a day

effects.log: You keep the book closed for one day, and let heaven surprise you.

events.text: The book rewrites itself true, and you are alone with it. {npc} is ringing the herald's bell somewhere for a gathering your pantheon already knew about. When {he} comes back {he} sees the steady new hand on the pages and sits down slowly. "So now it is never wrong," {he} says. "And I am."

choices.text: Ask {him} to keep the Calendar anyway

effects.log: "Someone has to ring the bell," you say. {npc} looks at you a long time and nods.

choices.text: Say heaven needs one true book

effects.log: "Then it has one," says {npc}.

events.text: The notebook has one page left, and it is blank. {npc} turns it over. "You could write yourself on it," {he} says, "and be the guide the next god finds." {He} smiles. "I hope the first tip would be kind. Something like: the herald is not your enemy. The ledger asks before you write."

choices.text: Write that line in the margin

effects.log: You write it small, in the margin, not on the page. {npc} laughs.

choices.text: Leave the page blank for now

effects.log: "Blank is fine," says {npc}. "I keep a blank day too."

events.text: {npc} keeps the blank day in the Calendar still. "If you wrote yourself on the last page," {he} says, "and tore it out, there would be one blank day in heaven for good. I would keep it." {He} closes the Calendar. "I would ring the bell on it. For nobody. That is a herald's way of saying sorry."

effects.log: {npc} opens {his} mouth, shuts it, and rings the bell once. For you.

choices.text: Say a blank day is a gift

effects.log: "It is," says {npc}. "Heaven needs one."

events.text: Ding! The Simulator becomes a loom. In Fate's house, under a roof of thread, {npc} works a great loom with the cloth of your domain on it. "Glimpses," {he} says, without looking up. "A miracle, a war of the heavens, a pantheon vote. A pinch of faith and I will show you how the thread runs. Not how it ends. I never show how it ends."

effects.log: {npc} lifts one thread. You see a miracle you have not worked yet, and the face of the child it saves.
"By cutting myself," says {npc}, and shows you a tiny scar. "Do not pull."
It is warm. It is everything you are. You take your hand back quickly.

events.text: {npc} of Fate's house stops the loom when you come in. "There is a cut in this cloth," {he} says, "where a god cut themself out, in another life, and left the domain to weave itself." {He} runs a thumb along it. "It has a little room for luck in it now. I always wondered who."

effects.log: "Then sit," says {npc}. "Glimpse. Do not cut yet." The first glimpse is free.

choices.text: Ask about the room for luck

effects.log: "It catches things," says {npc}. "Good things, mostly."

events.text: A glimpse: [A pantheon vote. The Will of Heaven votes to close the river of souls for a century.] You can see the thread that would tip it. {npc} sees you seeing it. "You can watch it run," {he} says, "or you can pull. Fate's house does not pull. You are not Fate's house."

effects.log: The vote goes as it goes. The river closes, then opens again early. {npc} nods.
The vote tips. The river stays open. Somewhere else in the cloth, a thread snaps.

events.text: A glimpse: [A war of the heavens, three years on. Your domain on the losing side.] {npc} holds the thread up to the light. "Fate is not kind," {he} says. "But it is fair if nobody pulls. You could ready your domain, or you could tie a knot in the war and change who loses."

effects.log: You ready your shrines and your faithful. The war comes and goes; you lose, and lose little.

choices.text: Tie a knot in the war

effects.log: {npc} looks away while you do it. When the war comes, someone else loses.

events.text: Watching is hard. You see a miracle you could work early and do not; you see a vote go wrong and let it. {npc} sits up with you on the nights you cannot sleep, and teaches you to weave plain cloth, no fate in it. "It helps," {he} says, "to make something that does not mean anything."

effects.log: It is crooked. {npc} wears it anyway, all winter.
{npc} lifts a thread for free. (A glimpse waits, free.)
It runs. It is beautiful, and none of it is yours to pull.

events.text: Pulled threads snap elsewhere. A goddess of the Green Assembly loses a harvest you did not mean to touch. The cloth of your domain is bright and lumpy with knots. {npc} picks at one with {his} needle, very carefully. "Every knot," {he} says, "I have to weave around. I am getting tired, {name}."

effects.log: It takes faith, a great deal of it. The goddess's harvest comes back the next year.

ok.log: You learn to weave around a knot. {npc} sleeps for the first time in a month.

fail.log: You make it worse. {npc} sighs and takes the needle back.

effects.log: "They do," says {npc}. "Badly."

events.text: Ding! A miracle, a war, a vote: all three glimpsed. The loom shivers, and the shuttle starts to run by itself, lifting threads for you to see with no faith asked. [The Domain Loom.] {npc} steps back from it with {his} hands up, as if from a horse that has learned to walk alone. "It trusts you," {he} says. "Do not make it sorry."

effects.log: You put your hand on the frame. It hums. {npc} smiles.
You watch the whole cloth run, free. It takes a year. You come out wiser.
You both sit and watch the shuttle. It is the quietest year of your reign.

events.text: The loom runs by itself, and its first free glimpse is of all your knots. {npc} watches the shuttle lift them one by one. "Look," {he} says quietly. "Every one of them, still holding."

effects.log: The shuttle shows you how. One knot loosens. {npc} breathes out.
They hold. The cloth is lumpy and strong.

events.text: {npc} holds up a pair of shears made of moonlight. "You have glimpsed your domain to its last thread," {he} says. "You could cut yourself out of the cloth and leave the domain to weave itself. There would be a little room for luck where you were." {He} puts the shears down. "Fate's house will ask you first. So will I."

choices.text: Say you like the cloth with you in it

effects.log: "So do I," says {npc}, and hangs the shears up again.

choices.text: Ask how much room for luck

effects.log: "About your size," says {npc}.

events.text: {npc} hands you the moonlight shears and keeps {his} hand on them. "If you cut yourself free," {he} says, "give these to me. I would never finish the cloth. I would just keep weaving around where you were." {He} lets go. "That is the ending, if the ledger lets you. It asks."

choices.text: Give the shears back for now

effects.log: {npc} takes them, relieved. "For now," {he} says.

choices.text: Say an unfinished cloth is honest

effects.log: "Most are," says {npc}.

events.text: Ding! [VILLAIN POINTS: fear in your domain.] Far below, a young hunter named {npc} stands on a mountain where your temple used to be and shouts at the sky. "You let my village flood!" The first stair of heaven appears under {his} foot. [A hero climbs to cast you down.] The System sounds delighted.

choices.text: Send {him} a vision of the flood

effects.log: {npc} sees the river that broke, and the dam no god built. {He} climbs anyway, slower.

choices.text: Send a trial: a storm on the stair

effects.log: {npc} clings to the stair all night. Your faithful below fear you a little more. (Villain Points rise.)
{He} climbs badly. {He} climbs anyway. You find you respect that.

events.text: {npc}, a hunter with a grudge, stands at the foot of heaven's stair and stops. "There is a song," {he} says, "about a god who left the throne open for a hero, and became the story heroes tell." {He} looks up at you. "I do not want to be in a song. I want my village back."

effects.log: {npc} stares. Then {he} starts to climb, a little less angry.
{He} climbs. The System counts the fear. It is less than it was in the song.

events.text: [Villain Points rise with fear.] The System wants trials: storms on the stair, beasts at the landings, a fall. Visions do not pay as well. {npc} is at the third stair, hungry and cold. A herald of {b10_pantheon} asks you, politely, whether you will crush the hero or teach {him}.

effects.log: You show {npc} the gods' side of the flood: the river, the old dam, the prayers nobody heard. {He} climbs, thinking.
A beast on every landing. The faithful below hear the roaring and fear you. [+VP] {npc} climbs anyway, bleeding a little.

events.text: {npc} reaches the fourth stair and finds a mortal village in the clouds, the souls of {his} drowned neighbours waiting there. "Go home," they tell {him}. "Or go on." You can send them a word to say to {him}. The System suggests a word. It is not a kind one.

choices.text: Have them say: we are well

effects.log: {npc} weeps on the stair for a day, then climbs on lighter.
{npc} climbs faster after that, and the fear below grows. (Villain Points rise.)

events.text: Visions pay little. Your domain fears you less every year; Villain Points come slowly; your pantheon calls you soft. {npc} climbs a stair a season, asking questions of the sky. "Why did the dam break?" "Why did nobody hear?" You answer as you can. On the fifth stair {he} sits down and asks: "Why do you let me climb?"

effects.log: {npc} laughs for the first time on the stair, and climbs again.
A wind on the stair. The faithful remember to fear. (Villain Points rise.)
{He} waits a long time, then climbs. Some questions are stairs too.

events.text: Trials pay. Your domain trembles; the Villain Points stack up like stones. But {npc} has stopped being a hunter and started being a hero, scarred and grim, and the mortals below sing songs about {him} against you. A priest of yours, Baek Ha-yun, writes up on the smoke: "Lord, the people are afraid. Is this what you want?"

choices.text: Answer Baek Ha-yun with a vision

ok.log: Ha-yun dreams of the stair and wakes understanding. The fear below gentles.

fail.log: Ha-yun wakes frightened. The fear below grows.

choices.text: Send another beast up the stair

effects.log: {npc} fights it on the landing. {He} climbs on. (Villain Points rise.)
Ha-yun prays twice more and then stops.

events.text: Ding! Six stairs climbed, and the fear of your domain is great enough to stand on. [The Fear of Heaven.] {npc} stands at the top step, looking at your throne, and does not draw {his} bow. "They fear you," {he} says, "and still they bring offerings. Is that what a god is?"

effects.log: {npc} lowers the bow a little. "I came to find out which kind you are," {he} says.
You stand. The whole of your domain feels it, and the faithful bring more. (Fear pays faith now.)
{npc} looks at the seat a long time, and sits on the top step instead.

events.text: The hero comes up the sixth stair scarred and furious, the songs of the mortals at {his} back. [The Fear of Heaven.] The faithful below bring more offerings than ever; they are afraid. {npc} raises {his} bow to your throne, then stops. "I thought I would feel better here," {he} says.

effects.log: You tell {npc} the whole of it, at last. {He} lowers the bow and sits down on the step.

ok.log: {npc} looks away first. The fear of your domain doubles.

fail.log: You look away first. {npc} nods, as if {he} learned something.

events.text: {npc} sits on the top stair with {his} bow across {his} knees. "You could let me take the throne," {he} says, "and be the villain every climbing hero is told of. I think the throne would be kinder with me on it. I think you would let me." {He} looks at you. "The sky asks first. I am asking too."

effects.log: "I would try," says {npc}.
{npc} nods. "Not yet is fair."

events.text: {npc}, scarred, stands by your throne. "If you left it open," {he} says, "and went down the stair I came up, nobody would see you again. The heroes would still climb. I would let them." {He} touches a scar a trial of yours left. "That is the ending you earned. The ledger will ask if you want it."

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. "Heard," {he} says.

choices.text: Say the stair goes both ways

effects.log: "It does," says {npc}. "I have walked it."

events.text: Ding! The ring is warm. Its old voice speaks, and for the first time it speaks of heaven: "I sat on a throne of Thunder once. Cheon Mu-gang, they called me. A god of {b10_pantheon} unmade me." At the next gathering a tall god in iron grey watches your ring from across the hall. {npc}. "So it found a new finger," {he} says.
events.arc: The Master Who Was a God

effects.log: "Because it deserved it," says {npc}. "Ask it what it did. It will tell you half."
[A divine lesson: how a god holds thunder without being burned.] Your hand tingles for a year.

choices.text: Hide the ring in your sleeve

effects.log: {npc} smiles, thinly. "I can hear it in there."

events.text: {npc}, a god in iron grey, stops you on the steps. "I have dreamt," {he} says, "of a god who gave this ring back its seat in heaven and went into the iron in its place. A child below found a warm ring after." {He} looks at your hand. "It is you again. I wonder if you will make the same choice."
events.arc: The Master Who Was a God

choices.text: Ask what the old master did to {him}

effects.log: "Ask {him}," says {npc}, meaning the ring. The ring says: "Later."

choices.text: Say you have not chosen yet

effects.log: "Good," says {npc}. "Then I am not your enemy yet."

events.text: The ring tells you half: Cheon Mu-gang ruled Thunder, and struck {npc}'s mortal city when it would not worship. {npc} unmade the Thunder-lord for it. "Teach me your method," you ask the ring. "Then take my revenge," it says. "Or make your peace with {him}, and I will teach you slower."
events.arc: The Master Who Was a God

effects.log: "Slower," the ring agrees, sulking. {npc} hears of it and frowns, as if peace were a trick.
The ring blazes. Lessons pour in. {npc} feels it across heaven and sharpens something.

events.text: {npc} comes to your temple alone, unarmed, which for a god of iron is a statement. "Give me the ring," {he} says, "and I will melt it, and it will be at rest. Or keep it. I only ask you to know what it was." The ring is very quiet on your finger.
events.arc: The Master Who Was a God

choices.text: Ask {him} to tell you, all of it

effects.log: {npc} tells you about the city and the lightning. The ring does not interrupt. Afterwards it is quieter.

choices.text: Tell {him} the ring stays, and goes on

effects.log: {npc} nods once and leaves. "Then I will be ready," {he} says at the door.

events.text: The slow method is slow. The ring teaches a lesson a year and sulks between. In between, you visit {npc}'s mortal city, which was rebuilt long ago and does not remember the lightning. {npc} is there sometimes, walking. "I come," {he} says, "to check it is still standing."
events.arc: The Master Who Was a God

effects.log: You walk the city's walls together. The ring is silent the whole way, which is a lesson too.
It refuses. Then, a year later, it says one word to {npc}: "Sorry." {npc} stops walking.
Your hands learn to hold lightning without the city knowing it was ever there.

events.text: Lessons pour in, and so does the ring's anger. You learn to hold thunder; you learn the iron grey god's weak places. {npc} meets you on the bridge of a gathering with {his} hands open. "I unmade a master who burned a city," {he} says. "Are you going to make me sorry for it?"
events.arc: The Master Who Was a God

ok.log: You strike; {npc} turns it aside. Neither falls. The ring is furious, and impressed.

fail.log: {npc} turns your thunder back on you. You stagger, singed, and the ring goes quiet.

effects.log: You lower it. The ring screams in your head. {npc} lowers {his} too.

choices.text: Ask the ring what it wants

effects.log: "To be a god again," it says. It is the first true thing it has told you.

events.text: Ding! Five lessons. The ring opens like a hand and gives you the rest of it: the whole method Cheon Mu-gang sat a throne with. [The Divine Method.] Thunder settles into you, patient. {npc} feels it across heaven and comes, not armed. "So it gave you everything," {he} says. "Did it give you the reason, too?"
events.arc: The Master Who Was a God

choices.text: Say it gave you the apology

effects.log: {npc} looks at the ring a long time. "Then it is a better ring than it was a god," {he} says.
It is enormous and very quiet. Your next breakthrough will have heaven's favour.

choices.text: Let {npc} hold the ring a moment

effects.log: {npc} holds it and does not melt it. The ring says nothing. That is new.

events.text: The method pours into you whole, and the ring roars for its revenge. {npc} stands across the gathering hall, ready, iron grey. Heaven goes still to watch. The ring says: "Now."
events.arc: The Master Who Was a God

choices.text: Close your hand on the ring

effects.log: You close your hand and hold the thunder in. The ring goes silent. {npc} lets out a long breath.
{npc} bows back. The ring sulks. The method is yours, and so is the choice.

events.text: {npc} walks with you on the walls of the rebuilt city. "The ring was a god," {he} says. "You could give it back its seat, and go into the iron yourself. Some child below would find a warm ring." {He} smiles, thinly. "It would be a better master than it was. I would make sure of it. The ledger will ask you first."
events.arc: The Master Who Was a God

choices.text: Say you trust {him} to watch it

effects.log: "I would," says {npc}. "For you."
"Then walk the walls with me another year," says {npc}.

events.text: {npc} sits down on the gathering hall's floor across from you and the ring. "If you went into the iron," {he} says, "I would go with you. Somebody should keep it company who knows what it did." The ring is very quiet. "The iron would be quiet too. The ledger asks first. It is a fair ledger."
events.arc: The Master Who Was a God

effects.log: "I know," says {npc}. "That is why I would."

choices.text: Ask the ring what it thinks

effects.log: The ring says nothing for a long time. Then: "Yes."

events.text: Ding! Four bars open over your throne: miracles, judgement, harvest, war. A scribe with ink to the elbows appears at your side with a tally board. {npc}. "Every bit of divine work you do," {he} says, "I tally. Ten marks and a bar turns gold. Gold gives you a perk. I have never seen a god turn one gold who did not cheat."

effects.log: {npc} makes a little note: honest, says they. {He} does not sound convinced. {He} sounds hopeful.
A sick ox stands up in a field below. {npc} marks the miracles bar. One.
"Small miracles, counted big," says {npc}. "Wars started to fill the war bar."

events.text: {npc}, a scribe with ink to the elbows, opens an old tally book and goes still. "A god once turned every bar of divine work gold," {he} says, "and laid the work down, and it went on like weather. The hand that tallied it was mine." {He} looks at you. "You have the same way of standing at a field."

effects.log: {npc} smiles and opens a fresh page. "Same rules," {he} says. "No cheating."
The marks are steady and patient. You recognise the patience.

events.text: The war bar is the slowest. Wars come rarely, and a god can only help end them. But the Throne of Storms and the Green Assembly are close to blows, and a word from you would start it. "That would fill the war bar," says {npc}, holding {his} brush still. "I would have to tally it."

choices.text: Keep the peace, fill other bars

effects.log: You make peace between them instead. {npc} marks judgement, and smiles.
The war comes. You end it in a season, and the war bar leaps. {npc} tallies it without looking up.

events.text: A dry year in your domain. You can work the harvest field by field, slow, so each farmer sees the rain come to their own row: Old Pak, the widow Kim, the boy with the two goats. Or you can work one great rain over the whole valley and have {npc} tally it as a hundred harvests. "It was one rain," says {npc}. "But it was a big one."

effects.log: Nine weeks of small rains. Old Pak cries in the row. {npc} marks the harvest bar nine times.

choices.text: One great rain, tally it a hundred

effects.log: The valley floods green. {npc} writes a hundred, slowly, and then underlines it.

events.text: Honest bars fill slowly. Gods of {b10_pantheon} with golden bars wave them at gatherings. {npc} brings the board to your throne every evening and reads the marks aloud, like a story. "Judgement, six," {he} says. "That was the river quarrel. You were very fair."

choices.text: Do the next piece of work with {him}

effects.log: You judge a quarrel between two villages, {npc} at your side. It is fair. A bar fills.

choices.text: Ask {him} about the other gods' bars

effects.log: "Padded," says {npc}. "All of them. I can tell by the ink."

choices.text: Listen to the story of the marks

effects.log: {npc} reads them all. It is a good story.

events.text: Big bars fill fast and wobble. The war you started is ended, but the Green Assembly has not forgiven it. {npc} tallies every mark you ask for, and writes something small in the margin each time that you are not allowed to read. One evening {he} leaves the board on your throne and goes home early.

effects.log: Every note says the same thing: true, but. You put the board down.

choices.text: Make amends to the Green Assembly

ok.log: The Assembly accepts a harvest gift from you. The war bar's marks stop wobbling.

fail.log: The Assembly sends the gift back, unopened.

effects.log: Another great rain. {npc} tallies it in the morning.

events.text: Ding! A bar turns gold. It glows on the board like a coin in water. [The Golden Domain.] Every other bar moves three steps on, as if the gold one pulled them. {npc} sets the brush down with both hands. "An honest gold," {he} says. "I have been a scribe for four thousand years."

effects.log: {npc} takes it and writes, in very small letters: done well.
The gold bar's gift settles into your domain like a warm stone.

choices.text: Go and see Old Pak's field

effects.log: It is green. Old Pak is asleep in it.

events.text: A bar turns gold. [The Golden Domain.] The other bars lurch forward three steps. {npc} looks at the gold a long time before {he} tallies it. "It is real gold," {he} says at last. "It was paid for a little oddly."

choices.text: Ask {him} to write that in the margin

effects.log: {npc} writes it. You let {him}. That feels like the start of something.
"It is," says {npc}. "That is what worries me."

events.text: {npc} lays the tally board across {his} knees. "Every bar gold, some day," {he} says. "Then you could lay the work down, and it would go on by itself, like weather. Nobody would have to thank you. I would stop tallying." {He} smiles. "I would miss it. The ledger asks before it lets you."

effects.log: {npc} goes pink under the ink.

choices.text: Say weather is a kind god

effects.log: "The kindest," says {npc}. "It never asks to be counted."

events.text: {npc} holds the board out to you. "If you laid the work down," {he} says, "lay it in my hands. I would keep the tallies, in a careful hand. Every mark true. Even the odd ones." {He} looks at the margin notes. "The ledger will ask. It is the only book that asks."

choices.text: Say {his} hand is the careful one

effects.log: {npc} nods, and writes it in the margin: careful.
"Not yet," agrees {npc}, and goes on tallying.

events.text: Ding! The jade warms. It is a letter, but not from ahead: it rises on incense smoke from below. A priest of a mortal line you blessed long ago, {npc}, writes in a careful hand: "Rain for our dry fields, if it please you." At the bottom: "Answer within four years, or I will think the line has been forgotten."

effects.log: Rain on the line's fields. {npc} writes back the next day: "Thank you. I did not think you were there."
There are forty years of them, in three hands. The last hand is {npc}'s. You find more time to answer this one.
It smells of pine and of the line's old house. You hold it until it cools.

events.text: {npc}, the last priest of a mortal line you blessed, writes up on the smoke: "Our grandmother said a god once sent themself down as the answer to a prayer, and was born to this line. We read the letter at every birth." At the bottom: "Is it you? Answer within four years, please. I am getting old."

effects.log: {npc} writes back in a shaking hand: "I knew it." Nothing else.

choices.text: Read the old letter they read at births

effects.log: It is short. It is in your hand. You do not remember writing it.

events.text: Two letters come up the smoke in one year. One is great: "A war is coming to our town. Turn it." One is small: "My niece has a fever." {npc} writes: "I know the first is larger. I only ask that you read the second." Your faith will stretch to one answer this year, maybe two.

choices.text: Answer both, the small one first

effects.log: The fever breaks at dawn; the war turns at dusk. Your faith runs thin. {npc} writes three pages.

choices.text: Answer the war, let the fever be

effects.log: The war turns. The niece recovers on their own, slowly. {npc} writes: "Thank you." Only that.

events.text: {npc} asks for nothing this year. The letter is only news: a wedding in a lean year, a roof mended, a boy lost on the road and found. "You do not have to answer," {he} writes. "I just like to tell you." The System notes: (No prayer. No time limit.)

effects.log: You send a warm wind through the wedding. {npc} writes back at once, delighted.

choices.text: Save the faith for a real prayer

effects.log: You keep your faith. {npc}'s next letter is a little shorter.

events.text: Answering everything costs. Your faith is thin, your shrines in heaven go short, and the gods of {b10_pantheon} ask why you spend so much on one small line of farmers. {npc} writes that the line has started praying for you, which no mortal line has done in an age. "For your strength," {he} writes. "You seem tired."

effects.log: {npc} writes back a recipe for a tea. You cannot drink it. You keep it.

choices.text: Ask {him} to give you more time

effects.log: {He} writes: "Of course. Take five years." (More time for a prayer.)
They ask. You answer the next letter.

events.text: Answering only the great prayers is efficient, and the line notices. Their letters grow shorter. One year none comes; then one, from {npc} alone: "The young ones say you are not there. I tell them you are busy. Are you busy?" The ink has run, a little.

ok.log: The young ones dream of a warm hand on the roof. Next year the letters are long again.

fail.log: The dream comes out muddled. They wake and argue about it.

effects.log: {npc} writes back three words: "I told them."
You wait. The smoke is thin that year.

events.text: Ding! Three prayers answered. The jade grows warm in your hand and the smoke from below thickens into a bright column. [The Line Kept.] {npc} writes: "The line flourishes. There are cousins in four towns. They all pray to you, and they are all very bad at it." At the bottom: a drawing by a child, of you, wrong in every way.

effects.log: You keep it by your throne. Gods who visit ask about it. You tell them.
A good year in four towns. Faith comes up the smoke every year now.
The second time you notice {npc} signed it with a little flourish, like {he} was proud.

events.text: The letters stopped, for a while. Then one more comes, after all the silence, in a child's hand: "I found an old shrine in the hills with your name on it. Grandfather {npc} says to write to you. Hello." (The Line Kept, late.)

effects.log: A warm wind in the old shrine. The child writes back every year after.
{npc} writes back: "I knew you were busy." It is very forgiving.

events.text: {npc}'s handwriting is shaky now. "The line will go on," {he} writes. "You could send yourself down as the answer to its last prayer, and be born to it. Grandmother always said a god would. I would like to have met you as a baby." At the bottom: "You do not have to. The ledger asks. So do I."

effects.log: {npc} writes: "One day is a good day." {He} draws a little sun.

choices.text: Keep the letter by the drawing

effects.log: The two sit side by side by your throne.

events.text: {npc} writes from a bed by the window. "If you sent the answer down," {he} writes, "send it in my hands. I would carry it to the next birth. You could stay in the letter. We would read you aloud." The ink is careful. "I forgave the quiet years. The ledger will ask you first."

choices.text: Write back: thank you for forgiving

effects.log: {npc} writes one more line: "There was nothing to forgive. Only to wait."

choices.text: Say you would like to be read aloud

effects.log: "Every birth," writes {npc}.
